title: Pointer Fundamentals
description: What a pointer is, the address-of and dereference operators, declaration, initialization, and NULL.
objectives: Understand what a pointer represents and why it matters in C
Use the address-of (&) and dereference (*) operators correctly
Understand NULL and why checking for it matters

content.heading: What a Pointer Is
content.body: A pointer is a variable that holds a memory address — the location of another value, rather than the value itself. Pointers are central to C precisely because the language has so few built-in abstractions: passing data efficiently to functions, building dynamic (resizable) data structures, and managing memory allocated at runtime all fundamentally rely on pointers. Every pointer has a type describing what kind of value lives at the address it holds (int *p means 'p points to an int'), which the compiler uses to determine how many bytes to read/write through it and how pointer arithmetic on it should be scaled.

content.heading: &, *, Declaration, Initialization, and NULL
content.body:
The address-of operator, &variable, yields the memory address where variable is stored. The dereference operator, *pointer, accesses (reads or writes) the value at the address a pointer holds. int *p; declares p as a pointer to int (uninitialized — holding a garbage address until assigned); int *p = &x; declares and immediately initializes p to point at x's address. Dereferencing an uninitialized ('wild') pointer, or one explicitly set to an invalid address, is undefined behavior and a very common crash source.

NULL is a special pointer value guaranteed not to point at any valid object — used to indicate 'this pointer intentionally points at nothing' (e.g., malloc() returns NULL on allocation failure, covered later). Dereferencing a NULL pointer is also undefined behavior (typically a crash, a segmentation fault, on most modern systems) — but checking if (ptr != NULL) before dereferencing a pointer that might be NULL is a standard, essential defensive habit in C code.

content.explanation: *ptr = 100; writes through the pointer directly into num's memory, changing num itself. The NULL check before the second dereference avoids undefined behavior.

keyPoints: A pointer holds a memory address, not a value directly; & gets an address, * dereferences one
A pointer's declared type determines how many bytes are read/written through it
An uninitialized ('wild') pointer holds a garbage address — dereferencing it is undefined behavior
NULL represents 'points at nothing'; always check for it before dereferencing a pointer that might be NULL
commonMistakes: Dereferencing a pointer before it's been assigned a valid address
Forgetting to check a pointer for NULL before dereferencing it, when NULL is a real possibility
Confusing & (address-of, applied to a variable) with * (dereference, applied to a pointer)
